newsitem.title: USA: Long-sought balanced budget plan in sight.
newsitem.headline: Long-sought balanced budget plan in sight.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican leaders in Congress on Thursday worked to put the final touches on a historic budget accord that he agreed to present to his Democrats on Friday.

Republicans generally embraced the budget as outlined by their leaders, and Senate Democrats warmed to the plan as details were presented by White House officials. However, the plan will face an uphill fight to win support from House Democrats.

"This is Robin Hood in reverse: huge tax breaks -- capital gains, estate taxes for the wealthiest in our society -- cuts, modifications in the cost-of-living adjustments for the working class and poor in our society," Massachusetts Democrat Edward Markey said at a news conference.
In an effort to bring a majority of his own party on board, Clinton agreed to discuss the balanced budget plan at the Democratic retreat in Baltimore on Friday afternoon.

No announcement on a final budget agreement was expected until Friday. White House spokesman Mike McCurry said budget negotiators would continue working. "We do not have an agreement. It is a complicated process. If you pull hard on any one string it may unravel," he told reporters late on Thursday at a Democratic gala that raised $4 million.

The budget provides a five-year blueprint for spending cuts across the government and $85 billion worth of tax cuts for families and investors. It is designed to carry out commitments made in the 1996 elections to bring the federal deficit to zero by the year 2002.
Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, who had objected to the secrecy of the budget negotiations, later said he could support their product.

"I don't want to sound too euphoric here until we've been able to see just what the results of negotiations are, but the framework that was explained to us today is certainly satisfactory," the South Dakota Democrat said.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and House Speaker Newt Gingrich continued negotiations with the White House in an effort to work out details, particularly on the tax cut proposals. "We're making progress," Gingrich said.
"You never can get an agreement until everybody is comfortable with what you are agreeing to," Lott told reporters. "A lot of it is trying to verify exactly what we are agreeing to."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters at his daily briefing that Clinton was pleased by the progress being made by negotiators, but he declined to describe the pact and said there was no agreement for the time being.

"He (Clinton) is encouraged by the progress that is being reported to him but at the same time there are some unresolved issues," McCurry said, saying negotiations were expected to run late Thursday and possibly into Friday.

Much of the government's savings would come from the Medicare programme for the elderly whose spending would decline by $115 billion through 2002. Savings of more than $20 billion over five years will come from the Medicaid health system that will face a per person cap on federal payments, adamantly opposed by governors. Other domestic programmes would be cut $68 billion and defence $80 billion off the amount that would have been spent if current policies were continued for five years.

Liberal Democrats said they expected domestic programmes such as education would take a heavy hit. "The apparent big loser in the end will be domestic discretionary, despite all administration assurances to the contrary," Representative David Obey, a liberal Democrat from Wisconsin, said. He predicted a majority of Democrats would not support it.
White House Budget Director Franklin Raines and White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles held several meetings with Democrats in the Capitol to explain the proposal.
"This is a good solid agreement for Democrats if we get it, we haven't gotten one yet," Raines said.

The conservative "Blue Dog" coalition praised the prospective agreement. The group held a news conference that they said was in part to counter the impression left by party leaders that Democrats did not support the White House negotiations. "We applaud the White House and Congress," Representative John Tanner of Tennessee said.

Republican leaders were pleased with the reception it found when they presented the outlines of the accord to their colleagues early on Thursday. The closed-door meeting erupted in cheers after leaders explained the budget outlines.
The major sticking point late on Thursday was Republican insistence that tax cuts not be spelled out in the budget but left to be written by House and Senate tax writing committees.

The tax portion of a budget pact was expected to include a capital gains tax cut, estate tax reduction and a $500 child tax credit, he added. Also likely to be included would be provisions for child health care and tuition, he said.
The Democratic White House and Republican Congress have been at loggerheads over the budget since Republicans won majority control of both U.S. legislative chambers in 1994.
